{{Short description|English surveyor and mathematician}}
{{Use British English|date=September 2014}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2026}}
'''William Leybourn''' (1626{{mdash}}1716) was an English [[mathematician]] and land surveyor, author, printer and bookseller.<ref name = "ODNB">{{cite web|url = http://www.oxforddnb.com/view/article/16623?_fromAuth=1|title = Leybourn, William|author = Sarah Bendall|publisher = Oxford Dictionary of National Biography}}</ref>
[[Image:William Leybourn.jpg|right|thumb|A portrait of William Leybourn, from "La Science de l'arpenteur : dans toute son etendue", by Dupain de Montesson]]

==Career as a printer==
During the late 1640s Robert Leybourn's press in Monkswell Street near [[Cripplegate]], London was occupied with books and pamphlets of a political, martial and [[Millenarianism|millenarian]] nature. He printed [[John Arrowsmith (scholar)|John Arrowsmith]]'s sermon to the houses of parliament, ''England's Eben-ezer'' in 1645, and his ''Great Wonder in Heaven'' in 1647. In 1646 he published a pamphlet ''A Defence of Master Chaloner's Speech'', and an early edition of ''The Marrow of Modern Divinity'' attributed to [[Edward Fisher (theologian)|Edward Fisher]]: in 1648 appeared ''The Differences in Scotland stil on foot'', and from 1648 an almanack or ''Moderate Intelligencer'' of military affairs entitled ''Mercurius Republicus''. Robert Leybourn gave the apparently fraudulent ascription to Sir [[William Davenant]] of [[Edmund Bolton]]'s historical poem ''London, King Charles his Augusta, or City Royal'' of 1648.<ref>T.H. Blackburn, 'Edmund Bolton's "London, King Charles his Augusta, or City Royal",' ''Huntington Library Quarterly'', Vol. 25 no. 4 (August 1962), 315-23, [https://www.jstor.org/stable/3816379?seq=1#page_scan_tab_contents (at Jstor)]</ref> He printed [[Joseph Mede]]'s sermon on St. Peter's prediction of the apocalypse, and a work called ''The Englishe Catholike Christian'' by one Thomas de la More, minister, followed in 1649.<ref>More details available at [https://quod.lib.umich.edu/e/eebo2/A82301.0001.001?view=toc Umich/Eebo/TCP II] (Full text requires login).</ref>

Into his industrious hands William Leybourn introduced the second year of his astronomical almanac, ''Speculum Anni'' for 1649, and also the important astronomical work he had written with [[Vincent Wing]], their ''Urania Practica'', together with their reply to the criticisms of Julian Shakerley. From this time forth the Leybourn press found its direction in the works of William Leybourn, and of Vincent Wing, and for a wide range of serious works of astronomy, mathematics, surveying, military matters, and the like. In 1650 was printed [[Richard Elton]]'s ''The Complete Body of the Art Military'', John Wybard's ''Tactometria, seu Tetagmenomentria: or, the geometry of regulars practically proposed'', John Chatfield's ''The Trigonall Sector: the description and use thereof'' and the two parts of [[Thomas Rudd]]'s ''Practical Geometry'', and also John Spencer's Catalogue of the Library of Sion House, as well as Leybourn's own ''Planometria, or the Whole Art of Surveying Land'' under the pseudonym 'Oliver Wallinby'.<ref>See [https://www.worldcat.org/search?q=kw%3ALeybourn&fq=yr%3A1630..1650+%3E&qt=advanced&dblist=638 Worldcat] for bibliographical details.</ref>

In 1651 William Leybourn entered into a business partnership with Robert Leybourn as a printer and seller of books.<ref name = "ODNB" /> Their extensive catalogue thereafter became one of the most important of its time in the publishing or re-publishing of such materials. The second and third (posthumous) editions of [[Samuel Foster]]'s ''The Art of Dialling'' (which first appeared in 1638), with additional materials, was an early success.<ref>S. Foster, ''Elliptical or Azimuthal Horologiography'' (R & W Leybourn for Nicholas Bourn, London 1654), [https://quod.lib.umich.edu/e/eebo/A40031.0001.001?view=toc] (Umich/Eebo).</ref> The press closed in 1666, following the [[Great Fire of London]] (in which almost the entire second edition of Wing's ''Geodætes Practicus'', 1666, was incinerated<ref>See [http://www.earlycorvettes.com/budsurvpics/pre1800/compressed/wing1666c.jpg title page]{{Dead link|date=November 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }} at the website of the Francois D. "Bud" Uzes Memorial Scholarship Fund.</ref>), after which William moved to Northcott in [[Southall]], [[Middlesex]].<ref name = "ODNB" />

==Career as an author==
In 1648, Leybourn wrote ''Urania Practica'' with [[Vincent Wing]], the first substantial compendium of [[astronomy]] written in the English language.<ref name = "ODNB" /> This was printed by Robert Leybourn in London. Leybourn's press also printed other books of Wing's such as ''Geodaetes Practicus''.<ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.surveyhistory.org/surveying_books_1600s_-_1700s.htm|title = Surveying Books 1600s – 1700s|author = Francois "Bud" Uzes}}</ref>

''Planometria, or, The Whole Art of Surveying of Land'' was a [[pamphlet]] written in 1650 by Leybourn and published under the pseudonym Oliver Wallinby.<ref name = "ODNB" /> Leybourn expanded this into a full book, ''The Compleat Surveyor'' which was first published in 1653, by his own press.<ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.fig.net/hsm/news/leybourn.pdf|title = THE COMPLEAT SURVEYOR William Leybourn 1657}}</ref> This was the first book published on the subject that did not contain an extensive argument justifying surveying.<ref name = "MCRAE">{{cite journal|title = To Know One's Own: Estate Surveying and the Representation of the Land in Early Modern England|author = Andrew McRae|journal = The Huntington Library Quarterly|volume = 56|date = Autumn 1993|pages = 333–357|issue = 4|doi = 10.2307/3817581|jstor=3817581|hdl = 10036/77862|hdl-access = free}}</ref> It outlined the various instruments used in surveying, and how they were employed.<ref name = "TEBEAUX">{{cite journal|journal = Journal of Technical Writing and Communication|volume = 29|year = 1999|pages = 209–253|title = Technical Writing in Seventeenth-Century England: The Flowering of a Tradition|author = Elizabeth Tebeaux|doi = 10.2190/0ET6-4V6N-KWLE-XJE1|issue = 3|s2cid = 144399024}}</ref> It remained one of the standard references in the field into the 18th century. It instructed property surveyors on the construction of property maps, and how to make the appropriate coloured inks for the maps.<ref>{{cite web|title = Book Reviews: The Compleat Surveyor, by William Leybourn, and The Practical Surveyor|author = Samuel Wyld|url = http://www.profsurv.com/magazine/article.aspx?i=973|publisher = Professional Surveyor Magazine}}{{Dead link|date=November 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> At this time, the use of private estate maps was starting to become fashionable, providing clients with satisfying coloured maps for their guests to view. The book also contains instructions on mathematical measures. The section on the use of [[Gunter's chain]]s as a unit of length shows early use of [[decimal]]s in surveying. Leybourn later expanded and clarified this in his 1657 work ''Arithmetick, Vulgar, Decimal and Instramental''.<ref>{{cite journal|title = Decimal Division of Scales before the Metric System|author = H. R. Calvert|journal = Isis|volume = 25| pages = 433–436|date=September 1936|issue = 2|doi = 10.1086/347092|jstor=225380|s2cid = 144038198}}</ref>

In 1669 Leybourn authored ''The Art of Dialling'', a book on the use of [[sun-dial]]s and [[astrolabe]]s in determining the position of vessels at sea. The contemporary expansion of the [[Royal Navy]] and [[Merchant Marines]] created a significant demand for such manuals, and ''The Art of Dialling'' was well written, easy to understand and cheaply produced.<ref name = "TEBEAUX" />

Leybourn's 1693 work ''Panarithmologia, being a mirror for merchants, breviate for bankers, treasure for tradesmen, mate for mechanicks, and a sure guide for purchasers, sellers, or mortgagers of land, leases, annuities, rents, pensions, etc. ... and a constant concomitant fitted for all men's occasions.'' remained widely printed longer than any other of his works. Over twenty editions were printed, and printing remained active into the 19th century.<ref name = "ODNB" />

==Career as a surveyor==
[[Image:Tenement Plans by William Leybourn 1683.jpg|left|thumb|Maidenhead and Wrastler's Court, drawn by William Leybourn, April 1683]]
Leybourn acquired a good reputation as surveyor of land, and was often hired to survey the estates of gentlemen.<ref>{{cite web|url = http://plus.maths.org/issue40/features/uphill/index-gifd.html|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20060928050433/http://plus.maths.org/issue40/features/uphill/index-gifd.html|url-status = dead|archive-date = 28 September 2006|title = Defying gravity: The uphill roller|author = Julian Havil}}</ref> In 1672, six years after the [[Great Fire of London]], [[John Ogilby]] hired Leybourn to lead a survey of London.<ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.oldbaileyonline.org/search/place/hyde_strype.html|title = Place Search 1674 to 1713: Strype's London Map}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.oxforddnb.com/public/themes/95/95647.html|title = Oxford DNB theme: The great fire of London|author = Stephen Porter|publisher = Oxford Dictionary of National Biography}}</ref> Leybourn identified the need for books that explained the techniques for measuring building materials that were widely accessible, both in cost and language. This was needed for both determining the extent of the damage from the Great Fire, and for calculating the cost of repairs.<ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.ilab.org/db/book899_11038.html|title = LEYBOURN, William; A platform for purchasers, a guide for builders, a mate for measurers|publisher = International League of Antiquarian Booksellers|access-date = 11 July 2007|archive-date = 7 October 2007|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20071007220527/http://www.ilab.org/db/book899_11038.html|url-status = dead}}</ref>

It was believed that Leybourn was the designer of the emblem of the [[Bridge House Estates|Bridge House Estates Trust]],<ref>{{cite web|url = https://www.crwflags.com/fotw/flags/gb-lond.html|title = City of London (United Kingdom)|author = Colin Dobson}}</ref> which was charged with maintaining the first stone bridge over the [[River Thames]]. The emblem, sometimes known as the "Southwark Cross" but correctly the "Bridge House Mark" may have been adopted by Leybourn from a mark used on surveying maps to denote properties of the Bridge House in the 1550s: an earlier version in the [[Museum of London|London Museum]] on a stone of the Bridge is dated 1509, and the modern version can be seen in use (before Leybourn's appointment) on the City sword-rest of 1674 now in [[Southwark Cathedral]].<ref>T. Sharp, ''The Origins and Development of the Bridge House Mark'' (Guildable Manor of Southwark publications 2007)</ref><ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.museumoflondon.org.uk/English/Collections/ArchaeologicalResources/ArchaeologicalArchive/ArchiveNews/FeaturedArchive.htm|title = Museum of London – Featured Archive|publisher = [[Museum of London]]|date = 7 June 2007}}</ref> The trust retains that emblem to this day.<ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.bridgehousegrants.org.uk/CityBridgeTrust/TheTrust/History.htm|title = The City Bridge Trust – The Trust – History|access-date = 11 July 2007|archive-date = 29 April 2007|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070429183228/http://www.bridgehousegrants.org.uk/CityBridgeTrust/TheTrust/History.htm|url-status = dead}}</ref>
